analysis.one_liner: Bars credit bureaus from reporting medically necessary medical debt and stops debt collectors from pursuing medical bills for two years.
analysis.headline: A House committee approved the bill on a 31–24 vote, but it sat on the House calendar for the rest of the term and never got a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop credit bureaus from putting any medical debt from a medically necessary procedure on a person's credit report, and would block other medical debts from being reported until they were at least a year old. It would also stop debt collectors from trying to collect any medical bill until two years after the first payment was due, and would require companies to tell patients their options before reporting the debt. The House Financial Services Committee approved it, but the full House never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with medical bills, including people whose insurance disputes, denials, or surprise bills leave them with debt they did not choose to take on. Their credit scores would no longer be damaged by medical collections, which affects their ability to rent an apartment, get a loan, or get a job.

how_it_helps.text: Credit reporting agencies would be banned from ever including on a credit report any debt from a medically necessary procedure, and from including other medical debt until at least 365 days after it was placed for collection [S3][S4].
Debt collectors would be prohibited from attempting to collect a medical debt before the end of a two-year period beginning when the first payment was due [S3][S4].

Before reporting a medical debt, the company would have to notify the patient that the debt is restricted from credit reports, that it cannot be reported if it is settled or paid in the meantime, and that the patient can check insurance coverage or apply for financial assistance [S3][S4].

The bill gives the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's director authority to extend protections for borrowers demonstrating hardship, such as people facing severe financial or personal barriers [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Debt collection companies, which would lose a two-year window to pursue medical bills; credit reporting agencies, which would lose medical debt as a category of data they report and sell; and health care providers and hospitals, which would lose the threat of collections and credit damage as a lever to get patients to pay.

drawbacks.text: Hospitals and providers would lose the threat of collections and credit damage as a way to recover unpaid bills, which could show up as higher charges or tighter financial assistance policies for other patients [S3].
Lenders would lose a piece of information they use to judge whether a borrower can repay, which could make some creditors more cautious about people whose debts are hidden from their reports [S4].

The bill relies on the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's director to define which borrowers qualify for extended hardship protections, leaving a key part of the protection to future administrative decisions [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit for patients is direct and large: medical bills, often from emergencies or disputes over what insurance covers, would no longer silently wreck credit scores or trigger collection pressure for two years. The main cost falls on collectors, credit bureaus, and providers, and some of it could eventually surface in higher prices or stricter billing practices. On balance the protections for patients outweigh those costs, though the two-year collection ban is broad and the hardship definition depends heavily on the CFPB director.

outcome.mechanism: The House Financial Services Committee approved it in December 2019, finally reported it a year later, and it sat on the House calendar until the term ended without a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced the bill on December 5, 2019, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee [S1][S2][S6].
The committee held markups on December 10 and 11, 2019, and ordered the bill reported as amended by a vote of 31 to 24 [S6].
The committee did not actually report the bill until December 15, 2020, almost a year later, as H. Rept. 116-653 [S3][S6].

The reported version was stronger than the original: it raised the collection waiting period from one year to two years and banned credit reporting of debts from medically necessary procedures outright [S2][S3][S4].
The bill was placed on the Union Calendar on December 15, 2020, but the House never voted on it before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S6].
The bill attracted no cosponsors over its entire life [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt collection companies and the three major credit reporting agencies are better off, because medical debt reporting and collection continued uninterrupted. Hospitals and providers also keep collections as a payment lever, while patients with medical bills saw no change.

industries.note: The bill would bar collectors from pursuing any medical debt until two years after the first payment was due, cutting off a large, profitable category of collections. Their business model depends on collecting these bills, which for patients means collection calls and lawsuits over bills they often did not choose to incur.

Credit bureaus would be banned from including debts from medically necessary procedures on reports at all, and from including other medical debt within a year. Medical debt is a major source of the collection data they compile and sell to lenders, landlords, and employers.

Providers lose the threat of credit damage and collections as a lever to get patients to pay medical bills, which could raise their unpaid balances. At the same time, patients who avoid credit wreckage are better able to stay customers and pay other bills.
